theme: Into your hands I commit my spirit
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 31:1-8. This is a prayer of refuge by David. Notice the rock and fortress language and the line that Jesus prayed from the cross.
settingTheScene: Psalm 31 is a psalm of David written in a time of distress, perhaps when he was hunted by Saul. It contains a mixture of confident trust, honest lament, and thanksgiving. The first eight verses are mostly trust. Verse 5 holds special significance because Jesus used it as his final prayer on the cross (Luke 23:46), and so did Stephen as he died (Acts 7:59). Many saints through history have prayed it at the end of their lives.
observation: “In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me!” (v. 1).
“Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me!” (v. 2).
“For you are my rock and my fortress” (v. 3).
“You take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge” (v. 4).
“Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God” (v. 5).
“I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction” (v. 7).
“You have set my feet in a broad place” (v. 8).
interpretation:
David begins with a plea built on God’s character: “In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me!” He appeals not to his own righteousness but to God’s. He asks God to incline his ear, to rescue speedily, and to be a rock of refuge and a strong fortress. Then he states a conviction: “For you are my rock and my fortress; and for your name’s sake you lead me and guide me.” God’s reputation is bound up with his people. Because his name is good, he can be trusted to guide.

The enemies have set a trap: “You take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge.” David is not just fleeing; he is looking to God to pull him from danger he cannot see.

Then the line that has comforted generations: “Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.” For David, it was a prayer of trust at a time of danger, committing his life into God’s hand. It is a daily prayer, like a rest at night. And since Jesus prayed it at his death (adding “Father”), it became the prayer of the dying. When Jesus said it, he was committing himself into the hands of the Father who would raise him. For the believer, to commit our spirit to God is to trust him with our life now and our death at the end.

David contrasts his trust with that of those who “pay regard to worthless idols.” Idols cannot rescue. He rejoices in God’s steadfast love, “because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul, and you have not delivered me into the hand of the enemy; you have set my feet in a broad place.” God sees, knows, and brings out into the open. The tightness of danger gives way to wide places.

Verses 9 to 18 turn to lament, describing David’s grief, his friends’ abandonment, and his plot-ridden enemies. There David says, “But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, You are my God. My times are in your hand” (vv. 14-15). The psalm ends with a call to the saints to love the LORD and to be strong and take courage, all you who wait for him (vv. 23-24).
connection: Luke 23:46 and Acts 7:59 quote verse 5. Psalm 18:2, 71:1-3, and 91:2 use rock and fortress language. Psalm 25:2-3 also asks not to be put to shame. Psalm 18:19 and 118:5 speak of a broad place. Jonah 2:8 also refers to idols. Isaiah 41:10 and Romans 8:31-39 offer similar assurance. 1 Peter 4:19 speaks of entrusting our souls to a faithful Creator. Hebrews 5:7-9 speaks of Jesus’ prayers. John 10:28-29 speaks of being held in the hand of Jesus and the Father. 2 Timothy 1:12 expresses a similar confidence in what Christ guards.
application:
Pray verse 5 tonight as you go to sleep, committing your spirit and tomorrow into God’s hand.

Think of a situation that feels like a tight place. Ask God to set your feet in a broad place.

If you are afraid of death, memorize verse 5 and remember who prayed it first.
prayerPrompts: Take refuge in God, and tell him why.
Commit your spirit into his hands.
Ask him to lead and guide you for his name’s sake.
